title: Greedy
summary: Make the locally best choice at each step when you can argue it never rules out an optimal answer.
lesson:
How it works
- A greedy algorithm commits to one choice at each step and never revisits it, so it usually runs in a single pass or after one sort.
- It is correct only when an exchange argument holds: any optimal answer can be rewritten to agree with the greedy choice without getting worse.
- Many greedy solutions track a running summary, such as the farthest reachable index or the current balance, instead of exploring every option.

When to reach for it
- The question asks for a minimum or maximum count of steps, groups, or resources, and choices made early never need to be undone.
- Sorting the input by one key makes the right choice at each step obvious.
- A dynamic programming solution exists but its state collapses to one or two running values.

Common patterns
- Reach tracking: keep the farthest point you can get to and extend it as you scan.
- Running balance: accumulate a surplus and restart from the next position whenever it goes negative.
- Range of possibilities: track the lowest and highest value a state could have when a symbol can mean several things.
- Smallest first: sort and always consume the smallest remaining value so it starts its own group.

Pitfalls
- Trusting a greedy rule without a counterexample search; small hand-made cases often break plausible rules.
- Forgetting the global feasibility check, such as a total that must be non-negative before any start position works.
- Choosing the wrong sort key, for example sorting by start when the argument needs the end.
- Letting a running lower bound drop below zero when negative values are impossible.
